articles.title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
articles.summary: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 1:37 PM PDT · October 18, 2026 Anthony Ha Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’ Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.

Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value.

And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study .

But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed.

The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.” If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications .

His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.

articles.title: Cloud of suspicion lifted from NIST curves
articles.summary: NIST published a set of elliptic curves for cryptography in 2000. The seeds for the curves were supplied by the NSA, and cryptographers suspected the agency may have installed backdoors in the curves. And not without reason: the NSA did insert a backdoor in the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator. Two days ago researchers at Anthropic […] The post Cloud of suspicion lifted from NIST curves first appeared on John D. Cook .
articles.full_text:
NIST published a set of elliptic curves for cryptography in 2000.

The seeds for the curves were supplied by the NSA, and cryptographers suspected the agency may have installed backdoors in the curves.

And not without reason: the NSA did insert a backdoor in the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator.

Two days ago researchers at Anthropic [1] showed that the NIST curves were not seeded with a backdoor.

The rest of this post will give the background necessary to appreciate this result.

The security of elliptic curve cryptography depends on the difficult of solving the discrete logarithm problem.

In the context of elliptic curve arithmetic, the analog of exponentiation is easy but the analog of taking logarithms is hard.

In general it’s not practical to compute discrete logarithms over large elliptic curves.

But it could be easy for someone with inside information to compute discrete logarithms if something about the curve was not “general.” Specifically, the NIST curves have the form y ² = x ³ − 3 x + b (mod p ) for various values of p [2], and the suspicion regards the choice of b .

For nearly all values of b encryption over the elliptic curve should be secure, as far as we know, but in principle someone could engineer values of b to weaken the encryption.

So where did the b ‘s come from?

Were they chosen in good faith ?

Concern over the choice of seeds, the b ‘s, grew following the Snowden revelations.

Daniel J.

Bernstein emailed Jerry Solinas of the NSA on September 6, 2014 asking where the seeds had come from.

Solinas replied in subsequent emails.

He said the seeds were generated by hashing the ASCII representation of a humorous English message, but he could no longer remember the exact message or the precise hashing procedure.

On October 5, 2023 Philippo Valsorda announced a bounty for reverse engineering the origin of the NIST elliptic curve seeds.

Two days ago researchers from Anthropic claimed the bounty.

Valsorda verified the results and awarded the prize.

It turns out Solinas found the curve seeds in good faith, but his memory had faded over the years since the curves were published.

We now know he used a date, not a phrase, as part of the process of constructing the seeds.

The NIST curves have some nice properties, such as enabling some clever tricks for arithmetic in their base fields.

But adoption of the curves has been held back over suspicion regarding their origin.

Now the curves have been exhonorated.

As Valdorda notes … this nicely completes the “rehabilitation arc” of NIST elliptic curve cryptography, which I would now personally recommend over Curve25519/Ed25519/X25519.

Just in time for them to be retired in favor of post-quantum signatures.

Related posts What is an elliptic curve?

Monero’s elliptic curve Lewis Carroll and zero knowledge proofs [1] This does not imply that LLMs are necessarily a threat to encryption.

The search for the NIST seeds required a lot of brute force.

Some cleverness was required in order to come up with possibilities to check by brute force, but even that is sorta brute force at a higher level of abstraction.

There has been speculation that labs are looking for weaknesses in cryptographic primitives and protocols, but that’s a different matter than searching for seeds. [2] The curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 are built over the field of integers mod p , where the number of bits in p corresponds to the number in the name.

The P-192 curve, for example, has as its base field the integers mod 2 192 − 2 64 − 1, a 192-bit prime.

articles.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
articles.summary: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
articles.full_text:
Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses.

Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items.

A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art.

Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them.

Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.

Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself.

Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire.

We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.

The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas.

As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.

The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port.

Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.

The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.

Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences.

Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.

Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday.

A winner was announced Thursday afternoon .

articles.title: LaTeX package for Pascal-like triangles
articles.summary: When I wrote about the harmonic triangle yesterday, I displayed the triangle left-aligned using fixed-width text because that was easier than producing the format you usually see for Pascal’s triangle and related triangles. 1 1/2 1/2 1/3 1/6 1/3 1/4 1/12 1/12 1/4 1/5 1/20 1/30 1/20 1/5 … I asked Claude to write a […] The post LaTeX package for Pascal-like triangles first appeared on John D. Cook .
articles.full_text:
When I wrote about the harmonic triangle yesterday, I displayed the triangle left-aligned using fixed-width text because that was easier than producing the format you usually see for Pascal’s triangle and related triangles. 1 1/2 1/2 1/3 1/6 1/3 1/4 1/12 1/12 1/4 1/5 1/20 1/30 1/20 1/5 … I asked Claude to write a LaTeX package to make it easier to create Pascal-like triangles and it did a great job, including handy features I didn’t think to ask for.

You can download it here: numtriangle.sty .

I used this package to create the more attractive display below.

Here’s the LaTeX code that produced the image above. \documentclass[border=4pt]{standalone} \usepackage{numtriangle} \NewTriangle{\Leibniz}{start=1, edges=1/\n, rule=\L - \P, fractions, format=\displaystyle, xsep=2.8em, ysep=2.8em} \begin{document} \Leibniz[rows=5] \end{document} I then compiled the code to an SVG file with the following. pdflatex leibniz.pdf pdftocairo -svg leibniz.pdf leibniz.svg Bell’s triangle is not defined in a way that the LaTeX package supports, but I can produce the triangle by listing the content.

I made the triangle left-aligned rather than centered just to show that this can be done.

The LaTeX code was the following: \ListTriangle[shape=left]{ 1; 1, 2; 2, 3, 5; 5, 7, 10, 15; 15, 20, 27, 37, 52} Here’s a particularly photogenic image, Pascal’s triangle with odd numbers highlighted, showing the Sierpiński triangle pattern.

The code to produce the image: \PascalTriangle[rows=16, mod=2, xsep=1.9em, ysep=1.3em, cell style={font=\tiny, minimum size=1.2em}, highlight style={fill=orange!40}]
